title: Correlation Coefficient
student_objective: I can use a technology-generated correlation coefficient to describe the direction and strength of a linear association.

concept_cards.title: r is between -1 and 1
concept_cards.content: The correlation coefficient r measures the direction and strength of a linear association. Its value is always between -1 and 1.

concept_cards.title: The sign gives direction
concept_cards.content: A positive r means the variables tend to increase together. A negative r means one tends to decrease as the other increases.

concept_cards.title: The size |r| gives strength
concept_cards.content: Values of |r| near 1 indicate a strong linear association. Values near 0 indicate little or no linear association.

concept_cards.title: Use the scatterplot too
concept_cards.content: Technology gives r, but always compare r with the scatterplot. Outliers, curves, and clusters can affect what a single number tells you.

sign.teacher_signal: Student confuses positive and negative direction.

magnitude.teacher_signal: Student uses the sign instead of |r| to judge strength.

meaning.teacher_signal: Student treats r as proof of causation or ignores nonlinearity.

items.prompt: Technology reports r=0.92. Is the linear association positive or negative?
items.tutor_behavior: Use the sign of r for direction.
hint_steps: Look only at the sign first.

solution_steps.explanation: The variables tend to increase together.

items.prompt: Technology reports r=-0.08. Which is best: strong negative, weak/little linear association, or strong positive?
items.tutor_behavior: Strength comes from |r|, not merely the negative sign.
hint_steps: That indicates little or no linear association.

solution_steps.explanation: Ignore the sign when judging strength.
The linear association is very weak.

items.prompt: A calculator gives r=-0.87 for hours of exercise and resting heart rate in a sample. Interpret the direction and strength of the linear association.
items.tutor_behavior: Separate direction from strength before interpreting.
hint_steps: So the association is strong and negative.

solution_steps.explanation: As one variable increases, the other tends to decrease in a strong linear pattern.

items.prompt: Three data sets have r=0.61, r=-0.94, and r=0.78. Which has the strongest linear association?
hint_steps: 0.94 is largest, so r=-0.94 is strongest.

items.prompt: Technology reports r=0.88. Describe the linear association.
Which is stronger: r=0.73 or r=-0.91?
A scatterplot is clearly curved, but technology reports r≈0. What should you conclude about the linear association?
items.tutor_behavior: Distinguish linear association from all possible relationships.
hint_steps: A curved pattern can have r near 0.
Conclude little or no linear association, not necessarily no relationship of any kind.

solution_steps.explanation: There is little or no linear association.
Correlation r does not summarize nonlinear shape well.

items.prompt: Can a correlation coefficient equal 1.4? Answer yes or no.
Which is weaker: r=0.18 or r=-0.67?

solution_steps.explanation: Smaller magnitude means weaker linear association.

items.tutor_behavior: Direction is negative but strength is weak.

solution_steps.explanation: Negative direction with very small magnitude.

items.prompt: Which is strongest: r=-0.86, r=0.58, or r=0.33?

solution_steps.explanation: Largest magnitude gives strongest linear association.

items.prompt: Does r=0.90 by itself prove that x causes y? Answer yes or no.
hint_steps: Association alone does not establish cause and effect.

solution_steps.explanation: A strong association can exist without direct causation.

items.prompt: If r is very close to 0, what does that say specifically about a linear relationship?
items.tutor_behavior: Use precise language about linear association.
hint_steps: r near 0 means the points do not follow a strong straight-line pattern.
There is little or no linear association.
